solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Green card? Not a road permit?

indicators.note: not here means the following words are taken away from the word card

parts.note: taken as written
to permit is to allow

explanation.surface: A question about whether a green card is really just a document that fails to let you drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' takes away the A and road abbreviation from the card word, leaving only C. 'Green card' looks like one immigration document, but 'Green' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone inexperienced and immature, a synonym pair.

clue.text: European noble raised strong point in support of prisoner

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece in support of another sits beneath it

parts.note: a con is a convict

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: an asset is a strong point or advantage

explanation.surface: A European aristocrat who championed a fortification on behalf of a captive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns ASSET into TESSA, and 'in support of' places it below CON.
explanation.definitionFit: A contessa is an Italian countess, a woman of noble rank on the Continent.

clue.text: Cause of one leering lasciviously?

indicators.note: lasciviously suggests something wanton and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written

explanation.surface: What might make a man ogle lustfully?
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of I plus LEERING gives the answer, and the whole clue also defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sexy underwear is just the sort of thing that provokes a lecherous stare.

clue.text: Too much on top

definitions.meaning: excessive, as in charging ... the odds
positioned above, as a blanket lies above a sheet

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both excessive and positioned above something else.

clue.text: Lecture about a fine fellow from platform

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece surrounds the others

parts.note: to lecture someone is to scold them
F is short for fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: Someone gives a talk on an excellent chap from the podium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts A, F and F inside SCOLD, after its first two letters. 'fine fellow' reads as a compliment but splits into two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A scaffold is a raised wooden structure, a platform, especially one for executions.

clue.text: Boxer inside holds on tightly to food

indicators.note: inside means one piece goes within another

parts.note: to grip something firmly, as a limpet does to a rock
a hitter is someone who punches, a boxer

explanation.surface: A boxer in the ring clutches tightly onto his snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' suggests a dog or fighter; here it is a puncher. 'inside' signals that the puncher sits within the gripping word.
explanation.definitionFit: Chitterlings are pig intestines cooked and eaten as a dish.

clue.text: Going mad about centre in Huyton dumping illegally

indicators.note: about means one piece wraps around another

parts.note: flipping, as in flipping one's lid, is going mad

indicators.note: centre in picks the middle letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone losing their temper over a central Huyton site where rubbish is dumped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the going-mad word round the centre of Huyton, a town near Liverpool. Fly-tipping is the British term for dumping rubbish illegally.
explanation.definitionFit: Fly-tipping is the British name for the unauthorised disposal of waste.

clue.text: Leader of opposition, thought highly of, made a speech

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: something rated is held in high esteem

explanation.surface: The opposition leader, well respected, gave an address.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a formal speech, so the past tense fits.

clue.text: Mislead daughter with dodge

parts.note: to elude is to dodge or evade

explanation.surface: A parent advises a daughter to deceive and evade.
explanation.definitionFit: To delude is to deceive someone into believing something false.

clue.text: French FC having a new back sent off

indicators.note: back means the pieces it follows are read in reverse
off means the letters of the word are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A French football club whose defender has been shown a red card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns A plus N into NA; 'off' rearranges SENT into NTES. 'sent off' reads as a football dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantes is a city in western France with a well-known football club.

clue.text: Shivering at chilly local government building

indicators.note: shivering suggests shaking, so the letters are shaken up

explanation.surface: Someone trembling in a cold civic office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shivering' rearranges the letters of AT CHILLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A city hall is the headquarters of a municipal council.

clue.text: Fine, down by bar, police maintaining order?

parts.note: fine as in slender or thin
feeling down is feeling blue
a bar is a line or stripe

explanation.surface: A list of an officer's penalties and a pub visit, ending in police keeping the peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine', 'down' and 'bar' each look like the vocabulary of a court or pub but are plain synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a metaphor for the police as the slender barrier between order and chaos, from their blue uniforms.

clue.text: Contest not finished yet

indicators.note: not finished means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: an event is a sporting contest

explanation.surface: A competition still incomplete so far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not finished' drops the last letter T from EVENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words intensify a comparison, as in 'even better' or 'yet better'.

clue.text: Door kept ajar by this may lead to unwelcome developments

definitions.text: Door kept ajar by this may lead to unwelcome developments

parts.words: Door kept ajar by this may lead to unwelcome developments
parts.note: a door is literally propped open by a small tapered block, while the idiom means a small first step that opens the way to worse

explanation.surface: Propping a door open might let in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a small concession that leads on to larger undesirable changes.

clue.text: A stud poker broadcast could send one fast asleep!

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: Watching a televised poker game is so dull it knocks you out.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparked out is British slang for unconscious or deeply asleep.

clue.text: Training aid shown in missing Hitchcock film

parts.note: skipping a class means missing it
Rope is a 1948 Alfred Hitchcock film

explanation.surface: Exercise equipment that appears in a lost Hitchcock movie.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipping rope is used for fitness training, especially by boxers.

clue.text: Dogs retailer's reared, I suspect

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dubious, signalling rearrangement

parts.note: the shop's word with its S counted as a letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper's dogs have been raised, one suspects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' rearranges RETAILERS, REARED and I; here the S of 'retailer's' counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Airedales are a large terrier breed from Yorkshire, so they are dogs.

clue.text: See 16
Scented oil, marvellous through end of shave

parts.note: brilliant means marvellous
in, as in coming in through the door

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A perfumed oil, wonderful at the finish of a shave.
explanation.walkthrough: BRILLIANT, IN and E (end of 'shave') in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Brilliantine is a perfumed hair oil used to give a glossy look.

clue.text: Relative stationed in Quantico (US Intelligence)

indicators.note: stationed in means sitting within the following words

explanation.surface: A family member posted to the US Marine base at Quantico in intelligence work.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across QuantiCO US INtelligence.
explanation.definitionFit: A cousin is a child of one's aunt or uncle, a family relation.

clue.text: Proceed quickly across river, small river

indicators.note: across means spread over, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: to steam is to move fast

explanation.surface: Hurry over a river, a minor one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'across' means the hurrying word spans the river letter, which goes in after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A stream is a narrow watercourse, smaller than a river.

clue.text: See 13
Get to know, briefly, a humorist

indicators.note: briefly means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: to learn something is to get to know it

explanation.surface: Become acquainted, in short, with a comic writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts the N from LEARN. Edward Lear was a Victorian writer of nonsense verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear wrote limericks and nonsense poems, a famous comic author.

clue.text: Parking with skill — and that's not all

parts.note: P is the map abbreviation for parking
art is skill, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: Parking skilfully is only half the battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A part is a portion, something less than the whole.

clue.text: Drive lost set point

indicators.note: lost means astray, signalling the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tennis player's drive loses a set point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' rearranges SET POINT. 'Drive' looks like a tennis shot but means hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an order to accelerate, as one might urge a driver.

clue.text: Living quarters surrounding a royal residence

indicators.note: surrounding means one piece goes round another

parts.note: one's place is one's home

explanation.surface: Accommodation around a monarch's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounding' puts A inside PLACE after its P.
explanation.definitionFit: A palace is the official home of a monarch.

clue.text: Talk idly about award — it doesn't make any difference

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round another

parts.note: to natter is to chat idly, British slang
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Gossiping about a prize is pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the chatting word round the award; OM, the Order of Merit, is a prestigious British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom saying something is unimportant or irrelevant.

clue.text: Force second lock

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Pressure applied to a second door lock.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress is force or pressure exerted on something.
